b: The WR Women's Chess Tour, organised for the first time by Wadim Rosenstein in 2026, has come to an end and has its first winner: at the end of a tournament series that travelled through Manila, Tokyo, Bangkok and Hong Kong before reaching the final in Stuttgart, Kateryna Lagno emerged victorious.

The final tournament took place at Rosenstein Palace. As in the qualifying events, a blitz tournament was played on day one and a rapid tournament on day two, both in knockout format. The time controls were 3 minutes plus 2 seconds from move 1 in blitz, and 15 minutes plus 10 seconds from move 1 in rapid. The blitz competition was played over four games, while rapid was played over half that distance - with an Armageddon game deciding the match in the event of a tie.
The following players had qualified for the final tournament in the capital of Baden-Württemberg:
The tournament opened with a match between the two Muzychuk sisters. After a draw in a rook endgame in the first game, an exciting battle developed in the four-game family duel.
"It was a little strange to travel all the way to Germany just to play my sister", said Mariya Muzychuk. "We could really have done that at home". | Photo: Lennart Ootes

After three wins for white, Anna had beaten Mariya 2½-1½ and thus qualified for the semifinal against Zhu Jiner. There, as well as in the final against Kateryna Lagno, Muzychuk won by the same score and secured victory in the blitz tournament. Muzychuk had gone 2-0 up and, after losing game 3, was able to hold the fourth game to a draw.
The blitz final between Kateryna Lagno and Anna Muzychuk | Photo: Sebastian Siebrecht
Lagno, who lost the final, had reached it by beating Vaishali Rameshbabu 2½-½ and Leya Garifullina 2½-1½.

Carissa Yip had an opportunity for revenge at the start of the rapid tournament: the previous day, she had been eliminated straight away by Zhu Jiner, the world number two among women players. As in the blitz, an Armageddon game was required to decide the match. Yip won game one, Zhu the second. In the deciding game, Yip won with black. In the semifinal against Anna Muzychuk, the American scored a 1½-½ victory.

Yip's opponent in the final had to go to Armageddon twice to advance. She first eliminated Garifullina and then Mariya Muzychuk. With both Muzychuk sisters losing in the semifinals, there was no second family duel, which in this case would even have been the final.
Carissa Yip won the rapid tournament. Kateryna Lagno reached the final in both disciplines and thus secured overall victory. | Photo: Lennart Ootes
In the final, Yip won game one and was able to hold a draw in the next encounter, in which Lagno initially managed to obtain an advantage but could not convert it into a win.
With two appearances in the finals, Lagno ultimately came out on top in the overall standings despite losing both finals, ahead of Anna Muzychuk and Carissa Yip:

Incidentally, the name Rosenstein Palace has nothing to do with the organiser's name, as explained on the tournament website: "Rosenstein Palace was built as a summer residence for King Wilhelm I of Württemberg according to plans by the Florentine court architect Giovanni Salucci. The foundation stone was laid in 1824, and the palace was inaugurated six years later. Rosenstein means rose rock. According to legend, the king chose this name because the rose was the favourite flower of his late wife, Queen Katharina. Since 1954, the palace has housed the biological collections of the State Museum of Natural History Stuttgart".
An example from this collection can be seen here: Carissa Yip (centre) and Mai Narva (right) are happy to be interviewed by Emily Rosmait against this backdrop. | Photo: Lennart Ootes
